title: 14 small business advertising ideas
summary: Before dropping 5K on Facebook ads, try these 14 low-cost ad ideas for small businesses and get a better ROI on your small business advertising.
body_markdown:
I spent years working with small restaurants and local businesses to help them grow—and, honestly, very few of them needed a huge advertising budget to drive business. Sure, you could invest thousands in paid ads, hire a top-tier advertising agency, and work with influencers to promote your brand. But you don't have to: there are plenty of free or low-cost advertising options that will attract website traffic and in-person visits.


You might think of advertising as referring only to[paid marketing](https://zapier.com/blog/selecting-advertising-platforms/) , like newspaper or[Google Ads](https://zapier.com/blog/google-ads-mistakes) . But other[marketing strategies](https://zapier.com/blog/marketing-strategies) —including ones you don't have to pay for—can be just as effective. So before dropping 5K on[Facebook ads](https://zapier.com/blog/facebook-ad-examples/) , try these 14 free or low-cost ad ideas for small businesses.

14 low-cost small business advertising ideas


## How to choose advertising channels for your small business


If you're chock-full of small business marketing ideas but don't know how to put them to work, here are a few factors to consider:


-


**Audience fit:** Cheryl Regan, the founder of[SEO Swansea](https://seoswansea.com/) , says, "\[T\]he best advertising channel isn't the newest or the most expensive, but rather the one that fits how local people actually make decisions." For example, one of her clients gets brand visibility from hosting free music events that build goodwill with the community. She also sees hyper-local clients like pubs get results from old-school flyers.


-


**Channel coordination:** Some channels play nicer together than others. For example, Yulian Hrab, founder of[Excella PPC](https://excellappc.com/) , insists that clients get a free Google Business Profile before he manages their Google Ads. According to Yulian, Google Business Profiles build a healthy base of organic visitors for Google Ads to work with.


-


**Extra fees:** Before you choose a channel, make sure the features you need are included in the plan you can afford. For example, you might need a paid plan to use a[free app's](https://zapier.com/blog/free-small-business-software/) integrations, even though its website doesn't mention it upfront. Read the pricing page from top to bottom.


## 14 low-cost small business advertising ideas


### 1. Claim Google advertising credits


[Google Ads](https://zapier.com/blog/facebook-ads-vs-google-ads/) can help you reach your target audience in search results or on other websites through display and search ads. And you can get super specific with it: for example, you could target people who live within 10 miles of your store or folks who search for the items you sell.


The problem, of course, is money. Paid ads can cost quite a bit—and while they usually have a solid return on investment (ROI), it's often too much for a small business to put down up front.


One solution: Google offers free ad credits to new Google Ads users. Right now, they're offering a couple different promotional deals—including[$500 in free ad credits when you spend $500](https://business.google.com/us/google-ads/) . Many hosting companies will also offer a few hundred dollars in free Google Ads credits. Use these credits to test advertising strategies and see if the ROI makes sense for your business.


**Automation tip:** As a Google Ads user, you can get more out of your spend with[2,000 free Zapier tasks per month](https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/30759982131213-Limited-time-offer-Use-Google-Ads-on-Zapier-and-get-free-tasks-for-6-months) for six months on eligible Google Ads actions.


### 2. Claim and optimize your Google Business Profile account


Your[Google Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038063) (formerly known as Google My Business) is a completely free tool that lets you manage how your business appears in Google Search results. If you're not sure whether paid search ads are right for you—or if you're working with a really small budget—your Google Business Profile can get you a similar level of exposure for free.


There's a lot you can do with your profile, but these are the basics:


-


Fill out all available information, including address, name, phone number, business category, and website.


-


Use key terms people are likely searching for in your description.


-


Include images and videos of the inside and outside of your business.


-


Respond professionally to customer reviews.


**Automation tip:** Use Zapier to[summarize new Google Business Profile reviews in Slack](https://zapier.com/blog/summarize-google-my-business-reviews-in-slack/) . Or install Zapier MCP into your AI assistant to fetch review info right in the chat window.


### 3. Use micro-audiences to stretch your ad budget


Yes, spending money on[social media ads](https://zapier.com/blog/tiktok-lead-generation/) will help you reach a wider audience, but you don't need to spend hundreds of dollars for each campaign. Platforms like[Instagram](https://zapier.com/blog/instagram-ads-cost/) offer incredibly specific options to help you target micro-audiences that cost less.


Here are some ideas for targeting smaller audiences:


-


[Custom audiences](https://zapier.com/blog/create-custom-audience-in-facebook-from-customer-list/) : Upload your email list, and target only those users. This method is ideal for promoting new products or offering discounts to customers you haven't seen in a while.


-


**People who are interested in your big competitors:** For example, a cake decorator might target people who like *Cake Boss* or Dairy Queen.


-


**A small age range** : If your ideal target audience is older or younger, make sure to target only those users.


-


**A specific location:** If you're a local business, target folks within a few miles of your store. If you're an online business, consider a local marketing campaign, so you can still use geographic targeting.


You should also make use of any *exclude* options, which let you exclude specific audiences, interests, or locations, as well as *budget scheduling* features, which let you dynamically increase your campaign's daily budget during higher-volume periods. And use built-in[AI tools](https://zapier.com/blog/ai-in-advertising/) , like Google's Smart Bidding and Meta's Advantage+ tools, to help you increase your return on ad spend (ROAS).


### 4. Apply for business awards


Taking out a traditional ad in a newspaper will probably set you back a few hundred dollars. But there's a good chance your city or industry has a "best of" awards program—and since someone has to win those awards, why not you?


Image source:[Best of Nashville](https://www.nashvillescene.com/bon/2025/)


Search online for "Best of \[your city\]" or "\[your industry\] awards." Applying is often free or only a few hundred dollars, and it gives your brand both online and print exposure. In local markets, winners are often featured in the local paper or invited to give demonstrations live on local news stations. That's a lot of publicity for the price.


It's easy to write this off if you're not a local business, but there are awards for every type of business—local or not. There are also cross-industry awards like the[Webbys](https://www.webbyawards.com/) , which recognize online excellence, and the[US Search Awards](https://ussearchawards.com/) , which recognize the best digital marketing campaigns.


Use your discretion and don't apply to every available award—otherwise, it'll start to cost some serious cash. Instead, focus on the awards that you think will get you exposure to your target audience.


### 5. Host classes or events


Hosting classes or events is a great way to get the word out about your business and, depending on how you go about it, pull in some extra revenue. For example, a social media management company could host a free webinar about a new platform, or a bakery could run a cookie-decorating class.


Start by deciding what your goal is for the class: do you want to increase[brand awareness](https://zapier.com/blog/how-to-measure-brand-awareness/) , drive leads, or actually make a profit? If you're using it for advertising, try keeping the class affordable or free, if possible.


To increase signups, use established platforms like Airbnb or[online learning platforms](https://zapier.com/blog/online-course-platforms/) like Udemy or Skillshare. That way, you have a built-in audience who can discover your brand, product, or services. You can also use the paid advertising tips above to increase your event signups.


### 6. Offer an online coupon


I have a love-hate relationship with online coupons like Groupon. I've enjoyed using them to try new businesses myself, and I've used them to drive foot traffic for clients. But coupons also tend to attract deal-seekers who have no intention of becoming repeat customers. And if you're not careful with the discount amounts, they can end up costing you money. (Most coupon platforms also take a cut of every redemption, sometimes as much as half.)


If you decide to give it a shot, here are a few tips:


-


Set a firm expiration date (120 days is usually good).


-


Make it for first-time customers only.


-


Limit the number of deals to one or two per customer.


**Automation tip:** If you give away coupons based on email list signups, you can automate the process using Zapier. You can, for example, set up a workflow that creates a coupon in WooCommerce when someone joins your Mailchimp list.


### 7. Pitch through Connectively and similar platforms


[Connectively](https://www.connectively.us/) ,[Qwoted](https://www.qwoted.com/) , and[MentionMatch](https://mentionmatch.com/) are platforms that connect media professionals with expert sources. Those experts can include business owners and industry leaders.


For example, a local reporter might be looking for fun summer camps to include in an article or for a quote about how small businesses are getting ready for the holiday season. You can use one of these platforms to respond to their pitch, and they'll include your quote or example in their story if it's a good fit. You might even land a[backlink](https://zapier.com/blog/how-to-get-backlinks/) in an online publication. It's a great way to get free publicity—and to build credibility within your industry.


**Automation tip:** Use AI to summarize your pitching opportunities for the day. Build a workflow that pulls email alerts from your chosen platform's address, summarizes them using AI, and adds the summary—or even a fleshed-out pitch—to your daily to-dos.


### 8. Send direct mail


Though you might think it's gone the way of the dodo,[direct mail](https://zapier.com/blog/create-loyalty-with-personalized-direct-mail/) is alive and well. It's more personal—and might give you a better shot at building brand awareness than an email.


As with most tactics for marketing a small business, sending snail mail is even more effective if you segment your audience. For example, after moving to a new house, I received a packet welcoming me to the neighborhood and offering me a discount on blinds and new windows. The ad mentioned my new house, so they were likely tracking public records and targeting new homeowners. In the age of personalization, hyper-relevant ads like this can be incredibly effective.


### 9. Partner with other local businesses


Advertising is expensive, so why not split the costs? By pairing up with another business, you'll spend less while increasing your reach to a new audience (theirs).


How you structure the[partnership](https://zapier.com/blog/developing-strategic-partnerships) will depend on your business, but start by looking for a business with an overlapping audience that isn't a competitor. A family restaurant might partner with a bowling alley to promote birthday bowling parties with catering from the restaurant. Or a women's clothing company could create a[brand partnership](https://zapier.com/blog/brand-partnerships-growth-strategy/) with a kids' clothing company to create "Mommy and Me" clothes.


### 10. Create a newsletter of useful ideas or jobs


Not all advertising has to look like advertising. Rather than just promoting your business, consider leveraging[content marketing](https://zapier.com/blog/good-content-marketing/) by creating an industry-specific newsletter where you share useful resources, strategies, or even job openings with your audience.


One of my favorite examples is from Aleyda Solis, an SEO consultant and speaker. Every week or so, she sends out a roundup of industry news that includes trending topics, new updates in the SEO world, as well as some resources she loves.


It's useful to me because I stay up to date on industry news, but it also establishes her as an expert in the field. Depending on your business, you might also share local events or job listings. Once you build an audience with your content marketing, you can then use it as another spot to promote your business.


**Automation tip:** If you have social media or email automations that alert you about certain topics for your newsletter, you can connect those apps to Zapier MCP and fetch specific updates right in your AI chat window.


### 11. Go to local events


If you're a local business, consider[joining local events](https://zapier.com/blog/small-scale-marketing/) , either as a sponsor, volunteer, or board member. For example, I recently took my kids to an event, and a local martial arts school had set up a tent and was giving away free (small) cotton candy for the kids. Laid on the table were brochures and signs about their summer camps and classes. Would I have approached the tent if not for the cotton candy? Probably not. But it worked.


Any kind of local event is fair game: farmers' markets, movies in the park, holiday parades, food festivals, craft fairs, you name it. Just make sure to offer something your audience will want to draw them in. Free swag and sugar usually do the trick.


### 12. Make use of your local library


Libraries are one of the few remaining[third places](https://www.vox.com/the-highlight/24119312/how-to-find-a-third-place-cafe-bar-gym-loneliness-connection) that are also totally free to access. They also often function as community hubs that offer classes and connect people to services—so they're a great place to let your community know about what you offer.


For example, if you're a children's clothing shop, consider partnering with your local library to run a clothing drive. Or if you want to host events or classes like I recommended earlier, consider using the library as a venue. And of course, lots of libraries have bulletin boards where you can hang up posters or pamphlets advertising your business.


### 13. Create a behind-the-scenes social media ad


[Social media](https://zapier.com/blog/best-social-media-management-tools/) posts that show what happens at your business have a ton of ROI potential, partly because they're cheap and partly because people remain, against all reason and logic, interested in watching other people do things on the internet. You can share your wins, challenges, or simply a day in the life. Then, once a post proves it can attract engagement, you can promote it to an ad and pretend this was the strategy all along.


The Northern Virginia restaurant Rice Culture uses this approach a lot, and their video on pumpkin spice teas is a great example of an Instagram Reel worth boosting. It gets to the point quickly, but it gives the viewer an up-close look at these drinks as insider knowledge.

### 14. Ask for honest online reviews


Your online business listings and social media pages show reviews front and center, meaning your customers can give you low-cost or free business advertising without anyone having to say "brand advocate" out loud. The trick is asking for honest opinions instead of paying for five stars.


For example, when I went to a new revolving sushi restaurant with friends, the staff asked us to leave Google reviews. While they gave us free drinking glasses for meeting a spending threshold, there was zero pressure to write anything in particular. They also made it easy by giving us a QR code to scan to leave a review.


**Automation tip:** Build an AI workflow that triggers when someone leaves a review on your Google Business Profile, scores the sentiment with AI, and sends a weekly sentiment summary to your team's Slack channel.
